utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. It's the case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, we ended up yesterday in a kind of a procedural debate on the use of the interviews given by Mr. Prstojevic. Before the Chamber finally decides whether and to what extent Mr. Tieger is allowed to confront the witness with the text of his interview, the Chamber first would like to make a few more inquiries. First of all, Mr. Tieger, the interviews, as we find them in the 22nd of November 2003, 27th of November 2003, and finally 6th of May of this year, do the transcripts fully cover all conversations that have taken place with the -- with the witness, Mr. Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They do. Obviously apart from greetings and any scheduling conversations that might have taken place but all issues of substance, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everything of substance is recorded and is in accordance with the rules and tape recordings are available?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you'll understand and Mr. Stewart also will understand that, of course, pauses and hesitations in answers et cetera cannot be read from paper but can sometimes be identified in tape recordings where a witness takes more time to answer or whether he starts an answer not giving it any follow-up, restart again. So there is a possibility for the Defence to check on such course of events during the interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that information. Then, finally, we might ask the witness himself as well, Mr. Tieger, but in the 6th of May interview, the short one, there is some reference to an illness which might have affected the memory of the witness in 1996, which is of course well before both the 2003 interviews and the 2005 interviews but have you any further information about it? Of course, if not, then we'll ask the witness about it, because it might be of some relevance for the issue at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll ask the witness about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, for the record, it just -- it seems to say the 22nd of November, 27th of November and finally 6th of May. I think the correct dates would be 26th, 27 and 28 November.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think there is just a mistake in the labelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was reading the heading. I was reading the heading, so the interviews that appear under the heading, "Interview with Prstojevic at Sarajevo field office, 22nd and 27th," so apart from whether it covers more days or other days even. Then Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom? We will first start with a few questions to the witness in relation to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour it has been terribly confusing. In fact the very first interview was on the 25th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes but most important is that it was November 2003 because that gives an idea of the time when these interviews took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, indeed, Your Honour. It's only that in Your Honour recording for the record the dates, I just wanted to say that that's where we start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's good that it's corrected for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we will continue with the examination, I would have a few questions for you which are related to something you said during your recent interview with the representatives of the Office of the Prosecution. It is recorded that when you were asked whether you knew who Avdo Hebib was, that you reminded those who interviewed you of two things and the first thing was that you suffered from a disease or a sickness in 1996 which was hit or something in this part of the head, you said, which "can medically be proven and which influenced a lot of my memory." First of all I'd like to ask you what exactly happened, what was the kind of disease or illness you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, I did not go into the medical side of things but in 1996, due to too much stress and tension and due to the after effects of a cold I think I had a kind of stroke and on the occasion of a French general from IFOR visiting when we opened a bridge across the river Zeljeznica at Vojkovici, that was built by IFOR, whilst I was giving a really brief speech to mark the occasion, I almost felt as if something had hit me in the left side of my head, and tears came out and started flowing down my face because of this incredible pain. I was taken to hospital straight away and apparently my blood pressure was abnormally high, 180 something, I can't remember, and I never experienced that, either before or after. But since then, I sometimes tend to forget things and I never suffered from that sort of forgetfulness before, and this refers to both my daily life and even important occasions such as today. So in case I get a cold or I go out in the rain or something and I get wet, I normally have this headache especially in the left side of my head. If we could have a CT-scan for my head, I suppose the diagnosis would be rather easy but due to financial problems I never investigated it because it costs a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you recently treated for this illness or at least for these symptoms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question is you say you forget sometimes things. Now, in your interview on the 6th of May of this year, you pointed at something you did not know precisely because on the question whether you knew who Avdo Hebib was, you said "it is known to me that he was somebody amongst Muslims who was highly positioned in the BiH MUP or Ministry of interior." It seems that your memory did not allow you to give any further details on Mr. Avdo Hebib. It seems from your answer that you were aware that your memory did not serve you to get to the detailed answer to that question. My question is when you experience that your memory is insufficient to answer a question, would you be aware of that? I mean, when you say I forget things, are you aware of not knowing any more something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of the fact that not only do I forget something but lots of things but in order to cooperate properly and in order to help establish the facts and the truth, I am doing my best in trying to provide as complete answers as possible and to remember everything I can. For example, in the 6th of May, when I was at this interview, I listened to about 20 phone conversations, intercepts, that is, that I was involved in. Out of those 20, well, there was only one that I could remember clearly and that I could remember in every detail. As to all the other conversations, I could tell I was the person talking because I recognised my own voice and I recognised the voice of the person I was speaking to, and I could reconstruct more or less the situation, the circumstances, and I could acknowledge that it did actually happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you always make it clear when your memory could not serve you to give the accurate answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever have the experience that looking back at a later stage, that you found that you had given answers to any questions or that you filled in gaps of your memory where you were not sure about whether these were correct interpretations, constructions, although you actually did not remember what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are about two such occasions, but on both occasions we are talking about interviews -- I think it was the interview that took place in November 2003, and on one occasion, it was the fact that I misspoke myself basically, and I corrected that mistake within the next hour, and then there was another case later on in the course of the same interview, I was complementing some information, and there are quite a few things that I'm trying to explain and I'm trying to remember. All the various circumstances surrounding a given event and then I was explaining the said event, and the same thing happened now on the 6th of May with reference to the situation at Nedzarici. Initially, I completely missed the point. When I first heard the intercept I gave a totally wrong interpretation because I thought it was in relation to something else and then I had to re-listen to it and listen very carefully and then I was able to establish what it was actually about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would any of the parties feel any need at this moment to address the issues we have tried to inquire into? That should be done in the absence of the witness. Is there any need for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Prstojevic, Mr. Stewart, taking off the headphones, when the witness said that he doesn't speak any English would that be sufficient or would you rather have him --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. On the footing that the witness really doesn't understand English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Tieger, that if that would be different that you would certainly have noticed and therefore I take it that we can rely upon the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no information to the contrary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Prstojevic, could you please take your ear phones off? Yes. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, just very briefly, Your Honour. It was, and we don't suggest it wasn't, it was entirely appropriate for Your Honour to explore with the witness whether in his view he always made it clear when his memory didn't serve him or whether he's had the experience of when he's given answers of where he wasn't sure and so on. That was entirely appropriate. With respect, however, Your Honour, I do submit that that's not an end of the matter, that it is extremely important then that the -- that the Trial Chamber should objectively assess those answers in the light of the sort of pattern that we do see in the interviews. And, Your Honour, in effect my submissions made yesterday are of course self-standing without regard to this issue. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. But this is an issue that might have some relevance for the other issue, and that's the reason why would we had to explore it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I'm 100 per cent with that, with respect. Although of course we were aware of this issue and it would have come up and we are grateful to the Trial Chamber for exploring it because it's in a sense much easier for the Trial Chamber to explore it discreetly sometimes than for counsel. But, Your Honour, it adds to that point. It increases the concern, the objective concerns, and the risks inherent in the sort of process that we do see in these interviews that I mentioned yesterday, that by a series of steps and no doubt we shall come to some of those in cross-examination, sometimes the witness is led to a very different place from where he started, and that risk is clearly far greater in the case of an interviewee whose memory is subject to some impairment of the type that he has indicated. So Your Honour, that's the additional submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, who can disagree with the proposition that the Court should objectively assess the answers in light of the questions asked, the other answers, the answers given in court, the opportunity to assess the demeanour of the witness, and the totality of the circumstances? And that's all we have been urging the Court to do throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it took us some additional attention to start with that. Perhaps I could then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like then to give some guidance to you, Mr. Tieger. The Chamber does not disallow you to use the transcripts of the interview to refresh the memory of the witness. At the same time, the Chamber would not like to end up in the situation where whole pages are read to him and just ask for confirmation whether that's true or not. The witness has testified that he stands with his statement. The Defence has an opportunity on the basis of the audio recording to see whether apart from what's on paper, whether there is anything that should need further attention in terms of hesitations, in terms of time taken. The Chamber is also aware that even if a witness says that he was always aware if he did not remember something, that that is not the final answer. It could well be that a witness, although feeling that he is aware, might not always have an accurate judgement on the actual situation. The Chamber therefore will be very cautious and very prudent in this respect and so therefore you are not disallowed to confront or at least to use the transcript in order to refresh the memory of the witness. But at the same time you're instructed to be as cautious in that respect and not just by reading whole portions of it and say isn't it, but try again to use the statement to a minimum to refresh the memory, and to see whether this triggers the memory of the witness to give his testimony on portions on the same subject which have not been read to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. If I can seek some slight further guidance on that, Your Honour, I understand the court's admonition to mean essentially that -- two things; number one it doesn't want vast passages of the transcript read out, both because it doesn't want that done as a forensic technique because this is not the place, and secondly, because it wants to have a fuller understanding of what it is the witness actually recalls and rather than an adoption of that which leaves the Court in not as good a position to assess the totality of the evidence. I take it, then, that references to portions of the transcript without reading out those verbatim passages is more in line with what the Court seeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For example, if a witness describes a certain event by giving three or four or five details of that event, of course you could present the five details to the witness and then say, is this what happened? You could also say, do -- in your statement we see that you said something about who was at the table. Do you still remember? Then see whether any of the other elements of his description come out from his memory at this moment. I hope that you understand the way -- so let's try to make it as much as possible fresh testimony rather than confirmed statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I understand, Your Honour. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps not to the surprise of the parties, if the Chamber feels that a different approach might give results that better assist the Chamber in making its determination, the Chamber will intervene when it thinks it's really necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I simply say, Your Honour, without going into detail we would suggest that the guidance that Your Honour has given, it's underneath some of the principles applied to both parties but it would inevitably apply differently in practical terms to the way in which the Prosecution should approach this witness with evidence in chief and the way in which the Defence would approach cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the -- any inconsistency in -- between testimony and statement could be addressed, could I say, a bit more vigorously by the Defence in cross-examination than it's done in examination-in-chief. Is that what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's along the right lines, Your Honour, if I may say. At this stage, in summary, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, although as a general principle, I would support that, at the same time, Mr. Stewart, given all the circumstances, even there, some caution would be needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope I don't always lack caution in these areas and I will do my very best to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps special caution in view of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Special caution, Your Honour. There was -- there was something else I was going to say but I'm just suffering a memory lapse. Oh, I know what it was. Your Honour, this question of the listening to the B/C/S audio, Your Honour, the most that realistically we are going to be able to achieve is that specific passages which do come up, for example, today, it may then be possible for Mr. Krajisnik who we think has the disc at the moment to look at those passages if they are important today. Similarly depending where we are tomorrow and so on. But, of course, Your Honours will appreciate that any further extensive listening to the audio version is out of the question over the immediate future when this witness is here this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all I think that especially since these will be B/C/S recordings -- I take it you have them, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There are recordings of the interview Your Honour that took place with translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So everything is in there for whoever speaks whatever language.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Krajisnik of course is fully aware of the issue. I mean, I pointed at some matters that could draw specific attention. So therefore -- and it's not to be said that if -- even if at a later stage such an issue would be brought to the attention of the court, it would be still useful to do it, even if not everything would have been dealt with during the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Just to put a marker down for that obvious practical limitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will take sometime, yes. Then I think we could ask the witness to put his -- to put on his earphones again and Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before we adjourned yesterday, we were discussing or you were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. discussing a meeting of a military security nature held before the 1st of April during which there had been, as -- there had been threatening rhetoric about what would happen if there was no agreement. And before we adjourned, I had asked you about the agreement, what was the subject of the proposed agreement, what was the -- what was it that had to be agreed on or something would happen, and I won't repeat what was said in court yesterday. And my simple question to you now is: Was that about the -- about whether and how to divide -- to ethnically divide Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was an agreement that our top political and state leadership was working on with the representatives of the Muslim and the Croat people, and attempts were being made to reach a peaceful and agreed solution for the state structure and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think one example of that is the so-called Lisbon Agreement and within that context, we should also look at this matter, unless such an agreement and such a peaceful solution were to come about, and in case an actual conflict, armed conflict, were to break out, certain political leadership and part of the people involved in the military side of things - and what I mean in the first place here is the then Territorial Defence - the idea was that we should be in a position to successfully withstand stand any kind of aggression, any kind of armed attack on our ethnic area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I understand the distinction between a peaceful solution and the use of force, but again, my question was addressed to the issue of the agreement and what was the subject of that agreement, and perhaps it may be helpful if I could just refer you back to your interview in November 2003 during which you had an opportunity to discuss the meeting at which threatening rhetoric was used, and you were asked about your understanding of what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you always refer to the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's page 107, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- of the sequential transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we have the two to start both, one being one out of 207, the other one out of 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's the -- I'm sorry, by sequential transcript, I mean the full range up to 207.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At that time, you said, in essence, it's division by hook or crook or in a peaceful manner or by force. So I wanted to ask you whether the agreement that may or may not have been reached was about division and that the subject of the discussion was whether division would take place by agreement or if not agreement then it would take place by force.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that interview, from the month of November 2003, in spite of the fact that I did actually use the term division, this is probably not the right choice of words because the talks that were held and that our state political leadership was involved in about an agreed structure for Bosnia and Herzegovina, well, it was about whether Bosnia and Herzegovina would remain within Yugoslavia and if it did not, what kind of structure we would have, what kind of territorial organisation and distribution we would have, and I believe that at Lisbon, they almost reached an agreement that the Muslim leadership in the end they backed away, but this, in the last analysis, would have been acceptable to Serbs. But I didn't at any point have the idea that the Serb leadership was planning any sort of armed activity in terms of achieving the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think that we did not do that, in fact. Our activities and the activities of our leadership were basically aimed at maintaining a situation in which we could protect the population from killings and massacres, and in this conversation, 093, that we looked at yesterday as well, we keep referring to special measures in order to ensure the safety of the population. Measures were being implemented in order to protect the population, and we had no previously planned activities which implied that we would initiate armed conflict in order to carve up Bosnia and Herzegovina in a way that would be inconvenient to us. I think that it is fully clear how the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that the Muslim officers and other dignitaries in their own books actually wrote and made a public admission basically that the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina started when they decided that it should start, according to their forward planning, as it were, and that we did not initiate it and that we simply defended ourselves and our homes and especially in those areas in which we were a majority -- in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we will be addressing some of those issues further on in our questioning. At the moment I'd like to move on to ask you some questions about the authorities and the military or police structures that existed in Ilidza in April and May of 1992. And in that connection, could I first have you presented with an exhibit which I believe is previously been used in court? It's the 16 April 1992 order by Bogdan Subotic. I think that actually needs a new exhibit number, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a new exhibit. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P791, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for Mr. Stewart's benefit I think that's item number 3 in the pile of documents you're reviewing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, P791 is a document dated 16 April 1992 and it's a decision addressing a couple of matters. The first is the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then there is a decision on other components of the armed forces and a decision that a state of -- "an imminent threat of war is hereby declared with general public mobilisation of the TO and the entire territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina ordered." Can you tell us if you know what the effect of this decision was and -- in Ilidza and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak about the territory of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza and in a way the Serbian part of Sarajevo, the Sarajevo Romanija region. That is what I'm well informed about. We received this decision in the municipality of Serb Ilidza. However, from the view point of the defence of the Serb people of Ilidza, this decision came late. It was adopted too late. Why? Because the Muslim leadership had proclaimed general mobilisation much earlier, and since, in my testimony here was something that I didn't spend even a minute preparing for because I'm very tied up back home, I maybe didn't mention that the process of preparations on the Muslim side had started much earlier, and we would have probably been killed with our throats slit and expelled if we hadn't done anything. So the Muslim leadership took their decision on general mobilisation and the commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt but my question is a little more focused than that and I apologise if I didn't assist you in the way it was asked. By this decision, were Territorial Defence units in the areas controlled by Serbs put under the command of the Territorial Defence? And did they thereby become units of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Ilidza, the units of the Territorial Defence had been mobilised earlier because the formal official in charge of Ilidza before the war was in his proper position and everything functioned well, and the decision that came only sort of approved and formalised the -- what we had already implemented on the ground and approved that our steps to prepare the Defence of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the chain of command for the units of the Serbian Territorial Defence in Ilidza? And that means from Ilidza up to the top levels of command.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to explain one thing here, namely the status and the field of activity of Territorial Defence generally speaking, in terms of the doctrine of the Territorial Defence and civilian defence in the former Yugoslavia, according to that doctrine, all enterprises, all companies, all institutions, all municipalities, had, in addition to the Yugoslav People's Army, whose units were supposed to repel the first attack against Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I'm going to interrupt you. The Chamber would like you first to answer the questions and only then, if any further explanation is needed, we'll ask for it or if at the end you say I'd like to give a further explanation, we will consider that. But the question was: What was the chain of command for the units of the Serbian Territorial Defence in Ilidza, meaning from Ilidza up to the top level of command. We would first like you to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up to the 11th of April 1992, the chain of command did not exist. What existed were only advisory meetings and briefings. Did I say 11th of April 1992? Yes. From the 11th April on, when General Subotic was appointed minister of defence, consultations with the Ministry of Defence and the minister himself began, and from that point on, the hierarchy was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was that hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's perfectly clear. When the minister of national defence was appointed for the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and certain people in the Territorial Defence were designated, our commander of TO staff in Ilidza was immediately linked through this hierarchy with them, and he had all the necessary consultations and instructions from the people from that ministry. However, if you allow me one more thing, from that date, the 16th of April until the 19th May, when the army of Republika Srpska was created, for the most part, in the area of Ilidza municipality, our staff of Territorial Defence organised our defence on its own initiative, with the verbal support and minimal, almost symbolic logistical support from the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question, Mr. Prstojevic? And I would also like you to focus very much on the questions and to first answer them. In an earlier answer, referring to this decision, you said that Territorial Defence -- units of the Territorial Defence had been mobilised earlier, and the decision that came only sort of approved and formalised what we had already implemented on the ground and approved that our steps to prepare the defence were correct. Now, the decision reads among others, command and control of Territorial Defence will be exercised municipal, district, and regional staffs and republican staff of the SBiH Territorial Defence. Was that what you had implemented already on the ground? That is, that the Municipal TO was subordinate to the District TO and the regional staffs and finally under the Republican Staff of the SBiH Territorial Defence? Is that what you had put in place already and which was formalised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said then I repeated now here, maybe in different words because I did not -- because I don't remember what exactly I said then, but it's the same thing. Our Territorial Defence Staff was only linked with the Republican Staff of Territorial Defence because we did not have the regional or any other level in terms of TO staffs. And the Trial Chamber needs to understand that the situation at the time down there was chaotic and confused. We had actually done everything prior to the decision, and the decision only formalised the steps already taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to be as concrete as possible. I do understand your answer to be that your municipal TO was hierarchically subordinated to the republican TO, where the intermediate levels were missing. I see you nodding yes. That's now on the record. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. There were no other levels. However, the staff of the Territorial Defence of Ilidza was headed before the war by the Serb -- by a Serb, and it only continued to work in the new circumstances of war, the same way it functioned for many years before the war. Therefore, we didn't have time to make any special preparations or prepare the units or any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, again, please focus on the questions, whether it was any different, if we would like to know that, whether it was different from before the war, we'll ask you. Please concentrate on the question, answer them, and then wait for the next question to be put to you. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you mentioned the commander of the TO staff, the minister of defence. Was the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina part of that chain of command and, if so, at what level?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's perfectly clear that the Presidency of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina was at the very top, above everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the commander of the Ilidza TO a member of the Serbian Crisis Staff of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he was in charge of TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, was a Serbian police force that was -- that is Serbian MUP, formed in Ilidza in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly whether the Serbian MUP and the Serb police were formed in the end of March or beginning of April, but it was formed and the hierarchy went from the government of Republika Srpska down to the MUP because MUP was not subject to the influence of local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say the government, again let me ask you whether the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of that chain of command and, if so, at what level?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is always implied that the highest body of government in the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina was the Presidency, and only then, at lower levels, come other bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So is this the case, as you understood it, it was the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; beneath the Presidency in the chain of command was the minister of interior and then down through the levels to the police officials in Serbian Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I'd like to play an intercepted telephone conversation dated 20 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. Transcripts have been provided to the booth, I take it? Mr. Tieger, is there a problem? Madam Registrar, the transcript would be? I do see it's already in evidence, Mr. Tieger; is that correct? On the list it appears as --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, you have it listed as item number? At least on my list, it doesn't show as already being in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see. It's number 5, 20th of April. Madam Registrar that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It will be Exhibit P792.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's for the transcript, and we'll have P792(A), and the translation will have P792(A).1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour we seem to be having some technical difficulties. I will have to move on and play that at a later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we leave the number as it is and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one last question about the Territorial Defence, and you may have alluded to that earlier, Mr. Prstojevic. When the VRS began to function, were the TO units merged or converted into VRS units?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about some other forces that -- well, let me ask you about some other forces with regard to Ilidza. Did various paramilitary units come to Ilidza in April and May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you name some of those groups for the Court, please? Tell us as many of those groups that came to Ilidza that you recall.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know why this is important at this moment, but if I remember correctly, I stated that in my interview. One of those groups is mentioned at the beginning of this telephone intercept. It's Brne's group. Some others like Bokan came to Ilidza for a short while, as well as some Chetniks from Zvornik, from Republika Srpska, and there were also some groups that simply went in and out of Ilidza, even Arkan's group spent two or three days in Ilidza. But we were not enthralled with their presence and they left Ilidza very quickly. I cannot tell you the exact date now but I believe that I have told you at some point around what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When these groups - and we'll discuss them in somewhat more detail in a moment - came to Ilidza, were they obliged to subordinate themselves to the army or to the MUP? That is, to the VRS or to the -- whatever form of Serbian army existed at the time, or to the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, the men from this group that is mentioned at the beginning of this conversation, from Brne's group, they were resubordinated to the MUP. From the 19th of May all had to be resubordinated to the army of Republika Srpska. However, nothing functioned very well if they were involved, and they were usually let go with a word of thanks and sent away because essentially they were only keen on looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the few moments before the break, let me ask you just a couple of questions about the group you just mentioned and that's Brne's group. Was Brne, Brne Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was he associated with the radical party in Ilidza? Was he one of the leading people of the radical party in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the radical party was established, I believe he was at the helm for a short while until a new leadership was elected, but I think he was always part of the Radical Party throughout the war. He is originally from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was his connection or the group's connection with Vojislav Seselj?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Radical Party was in a way joined with the Radical Party of Yugoslavia, and I think there must have been some coordination between them. In one of my earlier interviews, I believe I said that Mr. Seselj even visited Brne's group in Ilidza two or three times which shows to what extent they were connected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I see that you're looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Trying to be attentive to the Court schedule, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until five minutes to 11 and I would like to restore again the Chamber being perhaps one of the major wrongdoers to establish more discipline in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you mentioned Arkan's group coming to Ilidza. Who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was the leader of the group of Arkan's men who came to Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leader of that group was somebody I did not know but his name was Legija, and within that group there were less than 10 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, your question does not clearly appear on the transcript since your microphone was not activated. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I have to repeat the question because I didn't have my microphone on, and the question was: Did you receive Legija at the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just inquire how the witness got the witness if it doesn't come through Mr. Tieger's microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a possibility that -- I noticed that the microphone was switched on halfway so I could hear at least some of the question. So therefore, some people might have heard more from that very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour sees the point of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the interpreter's booth get it even though the microphone was not activated. Because if they didn't, then [Microphone not activated] ... get the question is my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the B/C/S booth and I'll now switch to channel 6, I think I have to do, could the B/C/S booth -- the B/C/S booth informs me that they heard all of it. So there might be another mistake -- the microphone was not on but perhaps some switch was on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's quite satisfactory for my purposes, Your Honour. You see why the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour if I could ask to have an intercept dated May 14, 1992, between Mr. Prstojevic and Mr. Gagovic played -- or Colonel Gagovic, excuse me. That's ET 04013862.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask a question, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask a question before this conversation is heard. Coming back to what has been said by the witness a moment ago, talking about these paramilitary groups. They all had to be [French interpretation on English channel]. What does it mean, Witness? Did they mean that had all to be resubordinated? Who gave them the order to be resubordinated or to subordinate themselves to the Republika Srpska's army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The armed forces of the Republika Srpska was set up on the 19th of May 1992. Some groups, such as Brne and Arkan's men, arrived earlier than the armed forces of the Republika Srpska. As a rule, those were paramilitaries who had to be resubordinated. Not because they wanted to, they wanted to act independently, to do what they liked, and mostly those were not very noble tasks. But the armed forces asked them to be resubordinated to them or to MUP. So this was imposed on them at Ilidza. As soon as they got to Ilidza they had to report to MUP or the brigade command and then the decision would be made as to whom they would be resubordinated, where they would be housed and in what way they would operate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But who took this decision in Ilidza? Who imposed to these paramilitaries to resubordinate to the army of RS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there was no need for any special decision, in fact. According to the preexistent rules and regulations before the war with regard to mobilisation, and that referred to all of the population, everybody had to be either encompassed by the military units or within MUP or they would be under the so-called work obligation. Combat units just could not exist outside the scope of MUP and the armed forces, and if whatever group wanted to act as a combat unit, they had to be within the framework of one of these two structures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, before we play the intercept just a quick follow-up to His Honour's question. Did all those groups, those paramilitary groups, who came and were subordinated to the military units or to the MUP participate in both defensive operations and offensive operations to liberate territory?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These paramilitary units mostly participated in defence operations, considering that at Ilidza we engaged in no offensives excepts for one case of active defence in the area of Otis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, apart from mostly, did they also participate in offensive combat tasks liberating part of the territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's answered the question. Mr. Tieger is picking out the first half of his answer. His complete answer makes the position clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I disagree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness answered the question by saying that mostly participated in defence with one exception, referring to Otis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And his answer indicated, as I read the transcript, offensive except one case of active defence. So I will ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to put a question about Otis, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the one operation of which you spoke, Mr. Prstojevic, and which you characterised as active defence, an effort -- an offensive effort to liberate territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is really getting quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not -- Mr. Tieger, if you would express yourself in terms of gaining territory, whether it's then offensive or defensive, it's -- and whether these are euphemisms or they are real characterisations of what it's all about, the Chamber will have to decide about that at a later stage but I take it you are thinking of gaining or regaining territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I may ask the question in a different way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Let's hope in such a way that Mr. Stewart does not object.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I want to refer you to a portion of your earlier interviews. That is reflected in the interview of May 2005 at page 6 of the second sequential version of the transcripts. I believe they go first 1 through 37 and then another portion that goes 1 through approximately 22. And that's page 6 of that second portion. On that occasion, Mr. Prstojevic, you were again discussing the paramilitary units and were asked what type of operational duties they performed, and you said that all those who came had to be subordinated to the para -- military units and to take part in the combat tasks, defensive or if we were liberating part of territory in offensive combat tasks. Can you tell the Court what you were referring to when you said that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "offensive," what I meant was active defence of Otis where fighting lasted between the 1st and the 6th of December 1992, and two Ilidza brigades participated, the Ilidza and the Igman Brigade and within the framework of the Ilidza Brigade, there was a group of Chetniks from Zvornik, from the Republika Srpska, and there were less than ten men within that group. So what I meant was the participation of those men in that particular combat operation. As to fighting at Otis, there are clear facts indicated that this was active defence, considering the data, indicating what the plans of the Muslim forces were. They had their elite forces there and also indications as to what extent they were basically penetrating the area of Ilidza and how many civilians were killed, in the fields and also in the urban centres of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could play the intercept now, please? And again, this is ERN number ET 04013862, conversation of 14 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Straight away. Hello. Leader. He. It is Prstojevic. How are you? Thank God I'm fine. If it weren't for this one mistake, I could be singing at the top of my voice. Well, fuck, mistakes, you should not have made mistakes. I know. We did not but the men made mistakes. They were not ordered to do what they did. Well -- Our movement is now a bit -- we cannot move with complete -- with that staff. Sorry? Complete hardware is practically immovable right now. Well, it is not my fault. That means that it is practically crossed out. It is not -- Please, I have manpower but I do not have hardware now. There is no -- he has manpower but he does not have hardware. That hardware should not have been wasted, that is. Yes. Where is that commander? Commander Popadic is there on the terrain, on the spot. At least two vehicles, two armoured personnel carriers should be replaced at this checkpoint. Fuck it. No crew, I do not need crew. I have the crew, I have everything. I have surplus manpower, that means -- Are APCs that arrived yesterday all right? Yes, the ones that arrived yesterday. Is there a tank that is in working order? You should pull out those APCs. You should not let them fall into enemy's hands. I do not know for sure if anything is in working order here. Two tanks, three APCs, and so on. I'm not sure for this checkpoint. Fuck. And those two from yesterday are with Arkan's men. Where are they? They are, probably, there's no ammunition for one of them probably -- Well, fuck everything. And where's that commander? I want to speak to him. Okay. I will call him to get in touch with you, just let me find him. Have him call me. Please. Okay. Bye."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, Mr. Prstojevic, can you tell the Court who the participants in this conversation are?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already commented on this conversation on the 6th of May this year. And let me stress once again that I don't recall this conversation. However, listening to my own voice and listening to Gagovic's voice and trying to place all this within the context of the military situation at the time, which is quite clear to me, well, of course I can admit to having participated in this conversation. So obviously I was at Ilidza and Lieutenant Gagovic from the corps command at Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know Gagovic's rank and where he stood in the hierarchy of the corps command?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear the translation of your question. I can't hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, perhaps you first repeat the question and see whether it goes any better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us Gagovic's rank and where he stood in the hierarchy of the corps command?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gagovic, as far as I can remember, was a Colonel, and he was one of the operatives within the Sarajevo army region. He was the second or the third in command in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the APCs referred to in the conversation that had arrived yesterday and that you indicated were with Arkan's men, can you tell us how Arkan's men received those APCs?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, Arkan's men got to Ilidza, I don't know by what route, on the 12th, in the evening. Late at night, in fact. As it was getting dark, I saw the commander of that group, Legija. He found me at Blazoj [phoen]. The following day, after they had spent the night there, they were walking around Ilidza, they took an interest in the structure of our territorial units, of MUP units, and they were housed at the Tama [phoen] Hotel that they chose themselves, and that was their independent post, as it were, as a unit, and as far as I know, they came by one of those vehicles. I think it was three-barrel one. And as to vehicles being referred to as being in their possession here, they were basically already situated in the area of the local community Kasindolska, where on that morning we actually suffered a terrible initial attack and those vehicles were not actually allocated to them as such, but Arkan's men basically took over the leading role over the territorial units in that particular locality. And they were particularly important in defending the area and pushing back the enemy units from that area. If the Trial Chamber allows it, I could perhaps explain a bit better. This was a horrible attack on the entire Serb area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I'd like you to answer the questions. The last question put to you, how did they receive the APCs, could have been answered relatively shortly by saying that they took over these or took control of these APCs during an attack launched at Kasindol. Whether there would be any need for further details is in the hands of Mr. Tieger, who will put additional questions if he would like to know more. Could you please very much concentrate on the questions and leave out any details you're not asked for, unless really of great importance. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As the Court will recall we had some technical difficulties with the 20 April, 1992 intercept which is 03290528 and we could play that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "100 is here and another hundred is to arrive. This Brne is a hell of a guy, really. Brne. There is ... Hello? Hello. Yes. Is Tomo there, Cedo speaking. One moment. Cedo who? Hello? Who is Cedo? An old ex-comrade of yours. Who is it? Is Tomo around? Who is Cedo? Who needs to speak to him? Is Tomo there, comrade? Yes, please. Tomo. Yes. Cedo speaking. How are you? Ah, Cedo. Listen, brother. Yes. A new piece of information has come in. Yes. All MUP executives -- Yes. -- went to the presidency with a single request, to be allowed to storm all barricades on the access roads to Sarajevo. Yes. So now they want a blessing and you should count on that solution that they will try during the afternoon or night hours. I see. So all those talks are now off. Pardon me? All those talks we had previously had do not count any more. Yes. Well, those people, they are trying to consolidate their positions. They will try a breakthrough, we don't know in which direction. It is most likely to expect them to try first through Ilidza. Yes, yes. They went to the Presidency with such a request, so that you know about it, man. Yes, I see. So the only request is to be allowed to make a breakthrough at all costs. I see. There. I see. So that you keep that in mind, for your orientation and further conceptions. I see. Well, I can't get through to Prstojevic. I haven't spoken with him. So if you talk to him, convey this message to him. Yes, yes, sure. Well, man. All right. Have a nice day. Goodbye."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, first could you tell the Court if you know who the participants in this conversation are?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recognise the voice of Tomo Kovac, and I do recognise the name of Cedo Kljajic who was one of the leading figures within MUP at Vrace, but I don't know him in person. I don't remember ever having met Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. him in person. The conversation is in line with the events at the time because after that conversation at dawn on the 22nd there was a horrendous attack on Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljajic, as he is dialing the number appears to be, among other things, praising Brne. Do you know what had happened around that time that would prompt such a remark?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, Brne, who was born near Pale and his paramilitary unit were situated at Vrace where Mr. Kljajic was, and in a part of Grbavica. This reference to 100 plus another hundred is incorrect. This is sheer propaganda and this is incorrect. However, at a later stage, through MUP, and I can't remember at what time, Brne came from Grbavica to the area of Ilidza through the Ilidza MUP. But this was after the 19th of May 1992. And upon request of the police commander from Ilidza, he was allocated accommodation in a motel in the area of Rakovica [phoen], where, according to my knowledge, he had between 20 or 30 people following him. The unit engaged in all sorts of things, pushing drugs and so on and they even killed one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kovac convey the message relayed to him by Mr. Kljajic to you. That is, that the MUP executives went to the Presidency to be allowed to storm all the barricades on the access roads to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tomo Kovac was a member of the Crisis Staff which met every evening and every morning, and I can't remember whether he conveyed that information or not, but it would have been normal standard practice for him to inform the Crisis Staff at every session of what was going on. However, there is one point which is incorrect here, that is to say that they went to request that. They were invited to carry out a task which had been determined as early as the 14th of April. That is to say, to carry out an attack on certain facilities, amongst other things the ethnic settlement in Ilidza, and the Chief of Staff of that army, BH, made that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So just to understand this, are you saying that it was not the case that the MUP executives went to the Presidency to be -- to seek permission to do so but that, in fact, they were tasked to do so from above?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I did provide proof for that in the course of the interview. Later on in 1996, they actually wrote about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you clarify who the witness is pointing at if he says "they"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, the Court would like -- when you said they were invited to carry out a task that had been determined as early as the 14th, who was to carry out that task? Who were you referring to as "they"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the members of the Muslim MUP, the MUP territorial units, the Green Berets and the Patriotic League, and to a certain extent the HOS units, and the European economic community monitors who were at the Serbia hotel in Ilidza at the time were informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that Mr. Kovac was a member of the Serbian Crisis Staff of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was the Serbian Crisis Staff of Ilidza subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staffs did not have a whole lot of hierarchy. I mean, there was no Crisis Staff for Serbs in the city of Sarajevo. It fell apart before it even started operating basically. And all coordination at the time was agreed with our leadership at the time. It was all coordinated with people who had been given certain jobs within the government of the Republika Srpska and the units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, there has been some reference to the leadership just now and I think previously. Can you tell the Court who the top leaders of the Bosnian Serbs were in 1991 and 1992? Who are you referring to when you refer to the leadership?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm just wondering that's not exactly the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fair. I understand the problem so let me re-ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask the question I asked initially. That is, who were the top leaders of the Bosnian Serbs in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think this Trial Chamber knows that very well. It was the people occupying the highest state positions in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and the highest political positions in the Serbian Democratic Party, considering that there was no other party protecting Serb national interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there any -- was there any single person or any one, two, three or four people who were the most important and most powerful leaders in Republika Srpska in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the trouble with these questions is that even the reference phrases like "the most important" and "most powerful" is just words. It gets all tangled up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, in your previous answer, where you said that the Chamber would know quite well who the leadership was, could you tell us by names who you considered to be among, as you said, the people occupying the highest state positions in 1991 and the highest political positions in the Serbian Democratic Party? Could you list them from top going further down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, at the elections in 1990, the Serbian member, the elected Serbian members in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina were Nikola Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic. They were our representatives on the Presidency. Mr. Momcilo Mandic was elected -- sorry, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik was elected president of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was our representative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. Could you please first concentrate on 1992, when the institutions of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not function well anymore and where the Serbian assembly and the later the Republika Srpska was established. Who did you consider to be the leadership of that new entity, and of the SDS? Please, from the top going further down. Whether they were elected or not, that's another matter. Just name them from the top down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is perfectly clear. Dr. Radovan Karadzic, Mr. Momo Krajisnik, Prime Minister Djeric, ministers of internal affairs and ministers -- the minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the names of the last two ministers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the names of the last two ministers you mentioned? That was the minister of internal affairs ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Momo Mandic. Later, Bogdan Subotic appeared as minister of defence. And as the government appointed new and new ministers, cooperation with them began in sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was twofold. First, state leadership authorities, and party. Would this list be valid for the party as well, or would that be a different list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radovan Karadzic was also president of the party, and later, the assembly also elected him president of the Serb Republic, or rather the Republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He had both hats, the political and the head of state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And under him, or next to him in the party, were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, an executive board was set up within the party, but at this time, there was an executive board that did not function, headed by Ratko Bozic. So for this period other people in the party did not matter. Those who mattered were people who occupied state positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your testimony well if you say that where the main board did not function, that next to or under Mr. Karadzic, the same persons mattered that were in the state positions you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. That is the case for March, April, May, June. There was a period from the beginning of the war until the end of 1992 when the party practically froze its operations until the Jahorina Plenary Session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One additional question. In the top state officials, you did not mention Mrs. Plavsic, neither Mr. Koljevic. Do you consider them not to be among the top state officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were indeed among the top state officials because they were elected at state elections in 1990. However, Professor Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic were less important and less influential as far as we were concerned, less important and less influential than other people, for the Sarajevo area because of the duties they performed, although Professor Koljevic spent some time in Ilidza in Hotel Serbia in 1992. We were more oriented towards President Karadzic and President Krajisnik, in terms of cooperation, for the area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And between President Karadzic and President Krajisnik, did one or the other have more influence or authority over the Sarajevo region? And if so, can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we take everything into account for the region of Sarajevo, Mr. Krajisnik was more important to us because we thought of him as a man who was born in Sarajevo and lived there and was much better acquainted with the situation, and would therefore understand us much better. Also, we thought that as Mr. Karadzic was very busy, Mr. Krajisnik would be more concerned about us. In simple terms, Mr. Krajisnik was closer to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, did Mr. Krajisnik's influence and authority in Sarajevo have anything to do with the people who were appointed to positions in that area?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, because he had influence over people holding state and public positions in the MUP, in the justice system, in the municipal bodies of Sarajevo, and other public institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And among those people, were some known in particular for their relationship to and for their close relationship to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to tell you much about it, but he certainly had closer relations with somebody who was his neighbour, who was born next door, than with people who lived a hundred kilometres away or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you first about both the power to appoint people and the power to terminate people. For appointment to positions in Sarajevo, did both Mr. Karadzic and Krajisnik have to give approval or one or the other or neither?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, we should distinguish between various levels of authority, of government. Neither President Karadzic nor President Krajisnik interfered or got involved in the election of officials into the municipal board of the SDS or municipal assemblies. However, that was in the period of 1991. But in the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and in other ministries, local municipal authorities had no say, so that commanders of police stations and chiefs of police were people we received without having any say in their appointment. When the assembly of the Serbian city of Sarajevo was formed, along with the executive board, then certainly the greatest influence on the election of civil servants was exerted by Mr. Krajisnik, and he had prior consultations and agreements with us concerning appointments of people like the mayor and members of the municipal government. There were certain bodies that I saw references to in your documents, such as war commissioners offices and War Presidencies, and even before them, war commissioners. These were appointed without any say on our part. Later on, in certain cases, we did get to have some say, not much, concerning the war commissioners' office, and later still, we lost all influence over the election of War Presidencies and war commissioners' offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For what sorts of positions, if any, was the approval of Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic required?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was quite clear about that. For instance, when municipal government was elected, the mayor of the Serb city of Sarajevo, and the prime minister of the Serb city of Sarajevo, there were talks and meetings attended by Mr. Krajisnik. There was no need for written communication. Views were harmonised at meetings. Certain key names were agreed. And that was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I asked earlier about terminations, although I didn't ask you specifically about that. Did Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik have the power to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't object the previous question but I am going to object now to the constant lumping together in the questions of Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic. Dr. Karadzic is not on trial in this courtroom and the last I heard he wasn't even in The Hague. Your Honour, Mr. Tieger did ask a question two or three minutes ago to invite the witness to draw some distinction between the positions of Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic and some distinction was drawn. But Your Honour, really, to ask in relation to both Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic is really two questions, every time, and it should not be put as a single question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It contains two, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it could be, if you're asked for what positions the approval of Mr. A and Mr. B were required, then you would expect an answer where both A and B would have to approve for that, and it would not give an answer to the question whether the approval of one of them was sufficient. So therefore, although I do not fully agree with your analysis of the question, it certainly assists the Chamber better if you split them up, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I fully agree with Your Honour's analysis of the logic. Of course, that's 100 per cent right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is invited to proceed in the way I suggested to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct this question, Mr. Prstojevic, to you in particular. Did Dr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik or both or neither have the power to remove you whenever they wanted?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is crystal clear. Had he wanted to, had Mr. Karadzic wanted to remove somebody from a position of local authority, he would consult Mr. Krajisnik and they could do that sort of thing at any time, although I don't know of a single case regarding local authorities such as municipalities. During the war, up to 1996, where certain officials were removed. In 1996, after the Dayton Accords, something like that happened concerning the mayor of the Ilijas municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, you referred earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said a while ago, when you talked about Mr. Krajisnik, I shall quote you, "he was better able to understand us because he was closer to us." So could you expand on that, please, and explain these two sentences to us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have already explained. Mr. Krajisnik lived in Sarajevo for ages. He knew everything there is to know about Sarajevo and the people who lived there. As a native of Sarajevo, he had special concern for the Serbs of Sarajevo and we could go to Mr. Krajisnik at any time. His door was open to us. We could be received for an interview. We could call him on the telephone. We could ask for help. We could ask for his advice. And the president was able to either praise or criticise our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us why? In other words, could you give us examples, or cases, when you yourself have been in contact with Mr. Krajisnik where he supported you and welcomed you in a friendly way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that all presidents of Sarajevo municipalities could give you any number of examples of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But I'm turning to you and I'm asking you the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically, as far as we are concerned, we had meetings and briefings with Mr. Krajisnik occasionally, and President Karadzic often attended them. Those meetings discussed the political and security situation. I think it suffices to say that we had regular meetings as required, sometimes even several times a month. And as soon as I would come back to my municipality from such a meeting, I could call up Mr. Krajisnik on the phone and ask additional questions and consult him if something remained unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will put my question to you again. Could you give us one or two or three examples which made such an impression on you that you were fully convinced that Krajisnik fully supported you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which example -- what kind of example would satisfy you. Well, let's take this. I remember one meeting which was attended by Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, General Mladic, too, plus some other representatives of the Main Staff of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. This meeting discussed the security and political situation in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. It also discussed cooperation among various bodies such as the army, civilian authorities, the MUP, and at this meeting, Mr. Karadzic happened to criticise me. At another meeting yet, Mr. Krajisnik praised Ilidza as a municipality that regularly submitted reports from various war commissioners' offices, et cetera, while others were not so diligent. I also remember some other meetings. For instance, when we were trying to reach an agreement about establishing the assembly of the Serbian city of Sarajevo, when we were trying to reach an agreement about the president of the executive board, Mr. Krajisnik held the view that the president of the executive board should be Mr. Maksim Stanisic. We from Ilidza, and I had headed that delegation, were angry with that man and we thought that in some critical times he had deserted Ilidza. He had simply fled. And we didn't want him. However, in the talks that followed, once or twice maybe in a period of 20 days, we accepted nevertheless the appointment of Maksim Stanisic to the post of president of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One additional question in this respect.
