You said, Mr. Prstojevic, that you remember one meeting, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and General Mladic being present, and some other representatives of the Main Staff of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. You say the meeting discussed the security and the political situation in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps security. What do I have to understand? Were any military operations discussed, or what do I have to understand as far as security is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know that it is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. extremely hard for you to understand because what was being told and what was being said to the public opinion was that Sarajevo Serbs had surrounded Sarajevo, and that they had kept it under siege. But the point is that about 200.000 of Sarajevo Serbs were housed and had to live in provincial parts of Sarajevo, at the outskirts of Sarajevo, and they were the majority there. And under war circumstances, in those areas in which the Serbs had the majority, they took those areas and that was by virtue of the fact that in some areas they had a 100 per cent majority, and for the most part, they engaged in defensive operations, they set up military defence lines along the borders of those areas. And we were constantly worried about whether we would manage to defend ourselves, because there were attacks from the city of Sarajevo, but we also had attacks from elsewhere. So we were surrounded twice basically. And it can be seen very easily if you look at the military map of Sarajevo. And everything we did was simply aimed at being able to survive and maintain and keep control of the territory that we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I do understand that you give now a description of the situation you felt you were in at that time. My question was: When you say "security issues were discussed at that meeting," I just would like to know what you discussed. Did you discuss tactical, strategic military matters, deployment of military equipment, deployment of troops? I mean, what were you discussing and then specifically in security terms with, for example, General Mladic, who was present at that meeting, or the representatives of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps? I would just like to get an impression of what you discussed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At such meetings, there were no discussions or there was no planning of military operations or military activity of any description. For the most part, we would report back from our own positions as to whether we found that our defence was stable, whether we had good cooperation with military commanders, whether the commanders and MUP were doing their job properly. But they, too, would talk about us. That is to say, they would report on whether the civilian authorities were providing them with the right logistical support. At such meetings there could have been, I don't know, requests for assistance, logistical assistance, or assistance in terms of providing food, clothes, arms, or in case we did not have an adequate army commander, we could ask for somebody to be appointed. In other words, whatever we expected the government to do by way of helping us, by way of helping our own local brigades, could be discussed there, and we could also discuss the way in which the hospital worked, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not objecting at all to Your Honour's questions, although Your Honour knows that I sometimes do. But this is not one of the occasions. But, Your Honour, two observations. One is that Your Honour's question was about a specific meeting. The witness's answer then referred to meetings generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll try to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I make one other practical suggestion, Your Honour? Since Your Honour's question is directed to a specific meeting it might -- rather than leave it till later, be helpful to the Trial Chamber and everybody if we could invite the witness to possibly date the meeting as best he can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first of all I asked about the meeting and the witness started his answer by saying "at such meetings." I'll ask for some clarification, then. Mr. Prstojevic, you mentioned a specific meeting Mr. Krajisnik, General Mladic, representatives of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps being present. In your answer you referred to such meetings. Can we understand that more meetings of that kind took place or were you referring to that one meeting only?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, there were more such meetings because the war went on for four years. There was a whole range of meetings like that. But on the occasion of that meeting in particular, at Pale, at the Famos premises, I can remember, if this is helpful, that the finance minister, a lady called Petra, was present there. And I know that Mr. Karadzic criticised Ilidza on some points, and I remember that I myself criticised the Finance Ministry with regard to their inspections and the fact that they set up the work of those inspectors, which is contrary to the way in which things worked during the war. So these were commercial affairs that we are talking about, commercial inspections, and it was the fact that these people were not accountable to anyone because their bosses were apparently at the central level and they could perhaps even not go to work or do anything at all for a month and nobody would say a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The meeting you just referred to as being held at the Famos premises in Pale, was that the meeting where Mr. Krajisnik was present as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other meetings -- you said quite a series of these meetings took place. Was Mr. Krajisnik sometimes, usually, always, or never present? Could you tell us about his presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, the meetings of the presidents of Sarajevo municipalities were held for the most part in the presence of President Krajisnik, as the man from Sarajevo. And I believe that he was absent extremely rarely. He was either there the whole time or for at least part of the meeting and I can't recall a single meeting where these matters were discussed that was not attended by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you situate those meetings, first of all the meeting you refer to as the meeting held at the Famos premises at Pale, could you tell us when that was? Month, year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, there was a whole range of meetings and I can't exactly tell you what month, but the meeting was in 1992. And I can indicate certain events surrounding that meeting, so on the basis of that, you could perhaps pinpoint the month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would briefly mention them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Maybe I should have my head examined actually because I have it all in my head. But even if I were totally healthy, I must say that it is not easy to pinpoint each individual meeting because we had dozens of them, maybe 50 or something, and all I can do is on the basis of these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said to me that you know for sure that it was 1992 and that certain events surrounding the meeting could assist us in further identifying the month. Could you please briefly tell what events you had in mind that could assist us? Just by mentioning them, without giving all details and further explanations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, if I could look at my papers, I could have course refer to each individual meeting, because I've got all my diaries, but I do know that a late Danilo Veselinovic at the time was importing peppers for Muslims in Sarajevo. It was like a humanitarian effort but it was also being sold and there was a great deal of uproar at Ilidza about these imports because it was suspicious because the population was unhappy, the armed forces as well, and the MUP, but we had to allow him to drive through and to drive peppers into Sarajevo on those lorries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a clear event you described. Do you know of any other such event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be much better if I were to check my diaries and be able to tell you what's what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my next question would be, could you give us a rough estimate on how many of those meetings took place approximately in 1992? I'm not asking for any precise number but please tell us it were three or ten or 25, approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two more significant meetings attended by the representatives of the armed forces. One was held at Jahorina and the other at Famos. At Jahorina, all brigade commanders in the area of Serb Sarajevo were present as well. As to other meetings of different nature or of a lesser scope, I think there must have been somewhere between seven and ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this is 1992? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I can only be really precise and specific if I can check my papers, and I did say before and I'm going to remind you again, that at Ilidza, I believe on the 17th of April, there was a meeting of a part of the government at the Crisis Staff and the meeting was about analysing the security and political situation and the possibility of having the government of the Serb -- of the Serb part of Sarajevo there, and the representatives of the government headed by Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were there, and all the Ilidza representatives headed by myself were there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're referring now two times to your diaries. These diaries are in your possession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They are. But I did say that I did not even have a single second to prepare for this testimony because I've got so much to do on my farm, and I have a very busy day. I work non-stop between 6 a.m. and 8 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I really appreciate that. Have you ever given access to your diary to representatives of the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. And I was not inclined to do so either, but I must say that they didn't even ask because I would have had to take some time to make sure I know what I'm giving them, because I did not enter information there in order to have some kind of account for later but it was mostly about day to day work during the war and the tasks that had to be carried out. And some things are written in a really nice and legible handwriting and others are just jotted down, and at any rate, I would like to keep that for myself, for family reasons, and to uphold family traditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the Chamber would invite you to give access to these diaries and if the Chamber would supervise that no personal family matters would become available to the parties but only those matters that are not family-related and not directly related to your personal life, would you agree to provide them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, when I mentioned family matters, there is nothing about my family in there. I would just like for my children to have my original papers when I go because I've got three children, and as the Trial Chamber -- and if the Trial Chamber, that is, asks for it, and if it is an obligation, we can make sure it is done, but I would need some time to go through all those papers and for them to be photocopied, and then I could make them available to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, the Chamber could take care of photocopying it and returning the original to you so that it would be available for your family members. We will consider the matter and I listen to your answers in this respect. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask another question based on your current testimony. You mentioned that [In English] "at such meetings there could have been, I don't know, requests for assistance, logistical assistance, or assistance in terms of providing food, clothing, arms, or in case we did not have an adequate army commander, we could ask for somebody to be appointed. In other words, whatever we expected the government to do by way of helping us, by way of helping our own local brigades, could be discussed there." [Interpretation] You said that Mr. Krajisnik, when he attended these meetings, listened to you very carefully. Does this mean that when you expected help and support, does this mean that Mr. Krajisnik had any impact on the decisions that were eventually taken? In other words, when did Mr. Krajisnik have a real decision-making power at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, it is only normal under such war circumstances would be for everything to be listened to very carefully. Mr. Krajisnik had the possibility to intervene directly with some ministers, to ask them to do this or that, which was in line with our requests, in case our requests were deemed to be justified, and in case they were deemed realistic and feasible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a second question to put to you, Witness. You said a while ago that Mr. Krajisnik attended these meetings, that he played a part, and that in these instances you could meet him, see him, and talk to him. But you also said that Mr. Krajisnik vis-a-vis people in Sarajevo and vis-a-vis you and people in Ilidza, you said that he was a very accessible man and in your testimony you said you could seek advice from him and you even mentioned the fact that you could phone him up personally to ask him for advice. Could you explain to us in what cases you had to seek such advice from him? When you ask for advice it's usually because you have a difficult question, it's usually because you hesitate over something. Do you remember any particular instance where you turned to Mr. Krajisnik to ask for advice from him, either personally or in his office, or over the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember certain talks about one matter or another. An area that was discussed very often where assistance was sought very often, was the supply of electricity for the area of Serb Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, sir. I'm not talking about material or financial support. You used the word "advice." You said you talked to him because you asked him for advice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course we could consult on a number of issues. As to whether it was about the economy, the infrastructures, and how we should solve things. I wanted to quote one example when we asked for a special electricity supply line between Pale Vogosca and Srpska Ilidza so that the population that had no electricity since August 1992 would get this electricity in 1993, and that, for example, had been done. And I do remember some more significant events as well. I mean, if there were some minor hitches, I can't really recall that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A while ago you mentioned these paramilitary groups that were doing bad things. Did you discuss this with Mr. Krajisnik, and when you asked advice, did you ask him what the role played by these paramilitaries might be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to paramilitary units, we never discussed those with Mr. Krajisnik, although I can't rule out the possibility that on the occasion of one of those meetings, since there were quite a few meetings, such groups were mentioned, because paramilitary groups would come within the area of competence of MUP, the police chief or the armed forces and a part of the Serb national state security. So that it went without saying that our state and political leadership had information on those groups, and since we were not favourably impressed by such organisations or rather such groups and the way in which they were organised because they would come and go rather swiftly, except for the Brne's group, they were locals and they stayed a bit longer. But we chased them away as well in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were -- they were sent away and they then went elsewhere. In other words, they were probably then involved in their activities in other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly what happened but in the case of Brne, as I said, he was in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. He then came to Ilidza and I think that in 1993, he -- well, at some point in the middle of that year, I think he was chased away from there and I don't know what -- where he ended up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, looking at the clock, I promise you that you'll be the one who puts questions to the witness after the break. We will adjourn until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the moment I'm getting French on the English channel. I don't know if that's a problem for anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's no problem for the Chamber but perhaps it's better to have English on the English channel but I, on 4, receive English only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Me too, Your Honour. I'd love to hear Mr. Tieger in French but I'm not getting that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll move forward. I'm sure it will be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, during the course of discussing the military-security meetings you mentioned that one of the issues that had been raised was whether commanders and MUP were doing their jobs properly. I'd like to next play an intercept dated 21 April 1992, ET 04014024.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it will be P794. We forgot to assign a number for the last intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you then assign a number to the last intercept, which was the.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 14th of May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 14th of May, Prstojevic and Gagovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P793.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should indicate that the English version contains a date January 21st 1992, but the B/C/S contains the date April 21st, 1992, which I believe to be the correct date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if there is any difference between the dates in B/C/S and English, what makes you choose the B/C/S date as a better one? Is it the context?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Context, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, context. So we will then see whether we could follow your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apology of the interpreters, we cannot find this particular transcript. Could we maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's number 2 on their list, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's number 2 on the list, Mr. Tieger says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's January 1992, on the list, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you found it meanwhile? Have the interpreters found it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honour, I'm sorry. It's a conversation between who and whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Conversation between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Prstojevic and it starts with an unknown male voice and later on -- no, it's all unknown male person.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, we have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Prstojevic: Hello. Unknown Male Voice: Yes. Prstojevic: Hi. Prstojevic speaking. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Unknown Male Voice: Yes, go ahead. Prstojevic: Is Garic there? Unknown Male Voice: Garic went to Pale. Prstojevic: All right. Who am I talking to? Unknown Male Voice: I'm one of his associates. Prstojevic: All right. This is Prstojevic speaking, commander of Crisis Staff Ilidza. Unknown Male Voice: Is that so? Prstojevic: Yes. Unknown Male Voice: So, Prstojevic, what's up over there? Prstojevic: Well, it's good. I sent them the help in manpower over there. Unknown Male Voice: We didn't -- oh, that's from Kasindol, right? Prstojevic: Yes. Unknown Male Voice: Yes, yes. We got that. Prstojevic: Where are they, tell me. Unknown Male Voice: But they are kind of scattered around. This guy told me that for the part that he received that some of them stayed and that there is about ten or his own men and the rest of them returned. Prstojevic: Tell me, are the fights still going on down there? Unknown Male Voice: Well, yes, but that's not very organised. The police doesn't want to come out and do their job. One part of the territory is already taken but the police doesn't want to come out so the people -- I don't know what to tell you. We have problems there. Prstojevic: Tell me how far will they go? Did you come to the left bank of the river Miljacka? Unknown Male Voice: Yes, this part is taken almost to the Miljacka river, but the upper part, even Krdelj street, that's still not taken. Prstojevic: And did you cut through Vrbanja? Unknown Male Voice: Yes. Prstojevic: And you in control there? Unknown Male Voice: Well, we are for the moment, but the police still didn't come out, so the civilians are holding that. Screw it. Prstojevic: Territorial Defence members? Unknown Male Voice: Well, yes. Prstojevic: All right, but the police should come out. Unknown Male Voice: Of course it should, but it's not coming ant [sic] that's the problem. So Krajisnik called him and he went up there so they can agree on them doing their job and if they don't want, screw it, they are not doing anything for the last 20 days. Prstojevic: They aren't doing anything apart from scratching their balls. Unknown Male Voice: Yes, man. Prstojevic: Well, they are slowing us down big time. Some pressure should be exercised on them. Unknown Male Voice: Yes, but how? Prstojevic: Well, let -- Unknown Male Voice: The only person who can do that is their minister and I don't think he's in favour of that. Prstojevic: Yes. Unknown Male Voice: It seems like that. Prstojevic: And is the minister up there on that number of theirs? Unknown Male Voice: I guess the minister is up there, yes. Up there with them. Prstojevic: All right. Have a nice day, man. Unknown Male Voice: You too. Prstojevic: Bye."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, just perhaps my knowledge of the English language is not sufficient. On page 2 first line, I see the word "ant," which I only know as a small animal but not as anything else. Is there -- is it a mistake or is it -- has it some special meaning? But it's not "ant" that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think you're right. I think that is a mistake and we can be happy to have that portion ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Translated perhaps by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It could be "and." I'm not doing an interpretation but it could certainly be "and," as a matter of English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But we can also read the B/C/S transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'm not solving the problem I'm just saying it could easily be "and." It makes perfect sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If someone could read the 7th box from the bottom of page 2 of the B/C/S, Mr. Karganovic has gone so he couldn't take over the -- perhaps he could -- do the interpreters have the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not -- yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could perhaps one of the B/C/S interpreters read aloud in the original language the 7th box from the bottom, which starts with ["B/C/S spoken] so that it will be translated into English?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to be a simple typo. It should be "and." Of course it should, but it's not, and that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the -- then it should be a D instead of a T. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, did you first of all -- do you recognise the unknown male voice on the -- or the voice that's listed as unknown on that intercept?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't focusing on identifying the unknown voice. According to the location from which this man was speaking, from one end of the town to another, I cannot identify the man. I don't remember this exchange. But I can identify my own voice. I know although superficially who Momo Garic is and I remember the events, as well as the assistance we lent to the territorial units over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That person indicated to you that Mr. Krajisnik called and he went up there so that he could agree on them doing their job. After he related to you issues about the police, do you recall whether that problem was resolved after the telephone -- after the conversation you had with this person?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how the problem was resolved. I only remember that we were supposed to lend assistance to territorial units locally. I remember we did that, and it was for that purpose that I had this exchange. A snag in this situation was the fact that members of the MUP were not performing their activities as they had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And apparently you both expressed concern about that, and did that -- did [inaudible] saw as a problem improve after your discussion with the unknown male person?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, it was a problem on the territory of another municipality, on the other end of town, and I had my hands full dealing with my own problems at the time. I wasn't going home at all, and I slept in my boots. And the very next day, there was the attack on Ilidza. It's very likely that after this one conversation, I didn't receive any more information apart from talking to people who were present in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, earlier you mentioned the war commission. In that connection I'd like to show you a document which is ERN number 03014405, which is item 22 on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Exhibit P795.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, P795 is an order on the establishment of a War Presidency pursuant to the decision of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska on 17 December 1992, on the cessation of validity of the decision on the appointment of wartime commissioners, et cetera. And it bears your signature on the bottom, or at -- so I take it that this then was an order that you made pursuant to the decision of the national -- of the Bosnian Serb Assembly? Is that correct, sir? Is that an order that you issued pursuant to the decision of the Serbian assembly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is completely correct, and we can see that from the preamble. Until that moment, the 16th of January 1993, there was in operation a war commissioner for the area of the Serb Municipality of Ilidza. When the circumstances changed and when the national assembly of Republika Srpska adopted a different decision, then we were duty-bound to set up War Presidency -- War Presidencies, rather, because the municipality was split in three parts. We had to establish these War Presidencies according to the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was the war commissioner in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, the war commissioner in Ilidza was Miroslav Radovanovic, and I think he was replaced by Jovo Mijatovic, national deputy, deputy to the national assembly, a man from Zvornik, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who tasked Mr. Radovanovic to be the war commissioner for Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our state and political leadership at Pale, Radovanovic was commissioner for Ilidza and Rajlovac, those two municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at the time he was tasked, was that by the War Presidency in Pale?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but I cannot recall now who appointed him and by which document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who comprised the War Presidency in Pale, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't know, precisely. But war commissioners' offices and War Presidencies were bodies that were supposed to be headed by people occupying the highest posts at a certain level. You can see that on the example of this War Presidency. People were not appointed by name but by their posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In your interview, you provided an assessment to 99.9 per cent of the people you believed to be on the War Presidency. What information -- do you recall that and, if so, what information was that based on? Was that based on their positions? Was it based on your knowledge of who comprised the leadership? What factors?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the functions discharged by those people. I don't know what I knew about that at the time. I cannot remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who did you assess as 99.9 per cent sure were on the War Presidency? I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I mean the War Presidency in Pale.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, the president of the republic should be there, president of the national assembly, possibly some vice-presidents, maybe Nikola Koljevic, the minister of defence should have been there. I can't name any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, what did you understand the -- or why did you understand that the -- that Mr. Radovanovic had been sent to Ilidza? For what purpose?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never quite understood why the municipalities in the area of Serbian Sarajevo were given commissioners when they had well-established local governments, municipal governments, and other bodies, but those people simply came, told us that they had been appointed, that they were superior to us, that they were going to follow the work of local government in the municipalities, the work of the MUP, the police and the army, the entire structure functioning in the area of a municipality. And I think -- in fact, I don't think, I know, that the last commissioner for us told us loud and clear that he would inform the leadership in Pale that the executive board and the local authorities were operating properly and that there was no need for his presence there. I can't remember the name of the man now. And that's what happened. He informed Pale and then he left. And later followed the decision of Republika Srpska voiding the decision to establish war commissioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the war commission of Ilidza submit records to the leadership?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they informed the leadership. I don't know all the ways in which they kept them informed. I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Radovanovic's political background and affiliation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radovanovic and Mr. Nikola Poplasen who was commissioner for Vogosca and Ilijas municipalities, upon coming to this area, started following the work of authorities. I don't know to what extent they belonged to the Serbian democratic party, but I know that they implemented the activities required for the establishment of the Serbian Radical Party. We did not interfere with that, nor could we. And I think that the first time a Serbian Radical Party was registered in our territory was in Ilidza, in the municipal court of Lukavica, and I know for a fact that their first communique concerning coalition parliamentary work was made over the radio, Ilidza Radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Radovanovic close to or associated with any of the top Bosnian Serb leaders in Pale?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. They were imposed on us by the leadership in Pale, so they must have enjoyed the trust of our leadership in Pale because they had been prepared as people who were trusted, people who were knowledgeable and superior to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there some people who were appointed to positions in the Sarajevo area who were known to be closer to Mr. Karadzic, for example, or Mr. Krajisnik, or any other Bosnian Serb leader?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened later, and such people arrived to occupy various functions when the executive board was established for the Serbian city of Sarajevo and when the mayor was to be appointed, when the local government for the Serbian Sarajevo was established. There were other, high-ranking officials appointed back at Pale who enjoyed their trust but they were appointed to republican authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was Jovan Tintor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger before you proceed, if you look at the question and the answer it's totally unclear what the testimony of the witness means. You asked whether people were appointed to positions who were known to be closer to Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik or any other Bosnian Serb leaders. So that could be anything. And then the witness said that that happened later. So it later happened, as far as I understand, that people were appointed who were closer to whomever Bosnian Serb leader. That doesn't assist the Chamber much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could be SDS and the other party. It's -- so could you please further explore that? I take it that you are trying to find out whether some people were appointed who were close to some specific Serbian leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In 1992, Mr. Prstojevic, some people appointed to positions in the Sarajevo area who were known to be closer to Mr. Krajisnik than to other Bosnian Serb leaders?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you name some of those people, please?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Names? Well, for instance, Jovan Tintor, Maksim Stanisic, Ljubisa Vladosic. Then Vojo Maksimovic, too. For the most part, it was Mr. Krajisnik who handled personnel issues for the Serbian Sarajevo. He charted the personnel policy as the person who was the most knowledgeable about the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was Mr. Radovanovic known to be someone who was more closely associated with Mr. Krajisnik than, for example, with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about a portion of your first interview shown at -- or found at page 32 of the November 2003 interviews, and just ask you to clarify that, if you can, please. You had first been discussing a man named Tomislav Sipovac, who came and introduced himself that Karadzic sent him for information jobs and coordinate with the top, and then you indicated that he was supposed to be the person through whom you would -- could communicate with Karadzic, but very soon, Mr. Radovanovic showed up and this person, Sipovac, was leaning more towards Karadzic as in contrast to Mr. Radovanovic who was leaning more towards Krajisnik. And I wondered if you could explain that.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said it at the time, I probably remembered better. It must be the case and I must have known why I said it. As to the previous list of names, there are other names as well at the local level such as Rajko Koprivica, who was the mayor of Vogoska and Bozic was the mayor of Rajlovac, et cetera. Tomislav Sipovac was sent to us in the way I described, but it is a man who I thought for a while was on the main board as well. But he was a writer, and I don't know how and why he never managed to strengthen his position, to consolidate his authority or whatever. I mean, he did what I said he did, and in the end, he was appointed as a director of one publicly owned company. I think it was called [B/C/S spoken], enlightenment, and I think it was to do with literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we turn next to an intercept which is dated May 14th, 1992, the ERN number is 04013853.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on your exhibit list under number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Number 10, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten. Madam Registrar that would then have number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It has already an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have not looked at the list. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not getting any English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can hear your voice now. Let's restart and see whether we ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Hello? Yes, good evening. God be with you. How are you? It will be better. Tell me --. Prstojevic speaking. I'd like to talk to Mrki. Mrki is not here. Mrki 2 is. Okay Mrki 2, then. Just a second. Yes. Hello, hello. Yes. Good evening. Good evening. How are you? Prstojevic speaking. I'm Mika's deputy. Yes, and your name is? Milenko. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Milenko? Yes. Why did Mika phone me? He phoned me [as interpreted] to check with you. These people in Kotorac -- Yes. What should we do with them? Did you arrest them? What did you do? People are down there -- oh, just a second, one second, (Milenko is telling the people in the room to be quiet). Yes. Hello? Yes. And where are those people? Have they been arrested? No. What then? Down there on the road, all of them. Men are separated from women. Ha. Just a second, just a second. Up there, right? He says men -- I've just received the word; men are in the Kula prison and women went in the direction of Butmir. Put Tepavcevic on. Here -- here is Novakovic. He will talk to you. It's Prstojevic. Stop fooling around. Hello? Hello? Hi Nedja. Hi. How are you. I'm fine. Have you been cleaning Kotorac today. They have. I don't know the exact details because I was engaged otherwise. Yes. Well, if you want we will call you later. Well, while. That's okay, but tell me please, I beg of you, why did you take women to Butmir? They said women were not in Butmir but -- But? Well, in Butmir, yes. Not to KP Dom but to Butmir. That's where they're going. They cannot go to Butmir. We'll mop Butmir in time as well. Aha. Butmir will be mopped up. Sokolovic will be mopped up. Hrasnica will be mopped up. Well, I don't know where to take them? They will all -- there is Bascarsija. Please, take them all to Bascarsija on foot. Aha. Aha. Women. Okay now I'll -- And men to prison. Okay I'll check with them now and then I'll let you know. Yes. Tell them those who convert to the Orthodox religion on the spot, they can stay, women and children. Aha. Okay, okay. Now I'll -- Do it, please, but don't make mistakes. You've done an excellent job but it means that Butmir will be mopped up in time. Tell that to the people there. Yes, yes, okay. There you go. Cheers. Okay."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, is that you speaking in that telephone conversation and to whom are you speaking, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this telephone conversation, I tried to reconstruct the events of 2003, and I can say one thing now, and I stick to what I said before. What is of essence here is that this was a conversation which did not take place on the 14th of May 1992, because this event did not happen on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And on what date do you believe this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the conversation took place on the 12th of May, late at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To whom are you speaking in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you can tell on the basis of the conversation is that I don't know who I'm speaking to. I asked to speak to one of the TO commanders who introduced himself as such. I think it was somebody called Mika Tusevljak, but then I asked to speak to the police chief at Kula straight away or rather, yes, the chief of police at Kula. I don't really know what his role was exactly. He was Miljenko Tepancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why did you want to speak to Mr. Tepavcevic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, it is the eastern part of Ilidza. From there, I was basically between 12 and 15 kilometres away from there, but in the course of that day, I had been further out. I was maybe 20 kilometres away at the far end of this municipality, in a local community there. And when I got there, somebody must have told me that certain activities had been decided there. As far as I know, the JNA, with the support of the TO units and MUP units, were involved. Basically, that part of that local community was a threat to the Lukavica barracks, and JNA, in order to protect themselves, and this can be seen here and without knowledge of the Crisis Staff, engaged in certain military activity and in the last analysis, they were entitled to do so. And I obtained information about that, and I was told that the civilians were sent down a road which is about 700 metres away, to a Muslim settlement, and there was another road going in the direction of Bascarsija, 300 metres away. The Dobrinja one, the centre of town Bascarsija, and that's why this was mentioned as the final destination, in order to determine the actual direction of that movement. I would just like to stress that the date is very questionable here, and it just could not have happened on the 14th of May because on the 14th of May we experienced the terrible attack on the entire western part of Ilidza and we incurred losses, 48 people were wounded and eight were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to put an additional question to the witness. Mr. Prstojevic, why could the women and children not stay on the territory of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, it's not the territory we are talking about. It's the fourth part or, let's say, a quarter of the local community and 100 or more, perhaps a thousand and a hundred inhabitants. If the JNA together with MUP and the Territorial Defence took it upon themselves to disarm the male Muslim population, the people who had already started to engage in some sort of activity, well, in that case, it would not have been usual for the women and children to be left behind, and they did not want to stay anyway, and they would have been very unsafe there because 300 metres away from that settlement was the urban territory of Dobrinja which was controlled by the Muslim forces and those people basically wanted to go there to join their relatives and so on, and also, perhaps, I should say that most -- that only very few Muslims came back to that settlement. Quite the contrary, they actually sold off their houses, et cetera, because most people want to live in cities these days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be different if they would have converted into Orthodox religion? Would they then have been safe or would they then have changed their mind or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We did not do that. This last bit is war propaganda, and it is a quote from a song, and it refers to something that took place in 1804, when Serbia was engaged in a war of liberation from Turkey, from the Ottoman empire. Apart from that, if you talk about the Orthodox Church, any conversion of other faiths, of -- from other religions into the Orthodox religion, is banned. But there is this phrase in an old song from 1804 and this has just been put into context haphazardly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, your remarks in this telephone conversation do not leave much margin open that you would consider the wishes of those who were on their way to Butmir and where you said they could not go to Butmir, seems not to be a lot of consultation with the persons, the women and children, involved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, I don't know. The only thing I do know is that this conversation took place after the job was done, and the conversation took place upon the completion of that task. Everything that had to happen happened before this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic says, "Well, I don't know where to take them, which is not language as if he had already delivered these women and children somewhere." And you answer to his question, "They will all -- there is Bascarsija. Please take all of them to Bascarsija on foot." That doesn't sound very much as if they had been taken to Bascarsija already, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I mean, whether they had gone or not but it was about 300 metres on foot. You can ascertain that even today. However, they did go -- I mean, I can't find it at the moment in this text but it is somewhere in the text. They had already gone, following the men who were being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see this on page 2, where Miljenko Tepavcevic who had a high-ranking position within MUP, he says, "I've just received the information now, the men are at Kula in prison and the women had gone to Butmir," in the direction of Butmir. And they went from the cross roads, they took a longer route, which is twice as long as the route I was referring to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- Mr. Novakovic says -- they said "women were not in Butmir but," and then you said, "But." "Well, in Butmir, yes. Not to KP Dom but to Butmir. That's where they are going." Then you say, "They cannot go to Butmir." And then Mr. Novakovic a while later says, "Well, I don't know where to take them," and then you say, "Take them to Bascarsija." That doesn't sound very much as if the whole road on foot has already been completed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there is a certain lack of clarity here as well, and the people talking to me don't actually know what's what but basically, all this population was within the area of responsibility of MUP, and the MUP people would know what they did there, and I can state that any use of means of transport for a distance of 300 or even 700 metres at that time could not have been organised because, I mean, you walk a kilometre on foot in seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prstojevic, the issue is not the means of transportation. The issue is who decides where people will go. Judge Hanoteau has one question for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to you pick up on this sentence, [In English] "Orthodox religion on the spot, they can stay women and children." [Interpretation] What did you mean when you said this? You talked about a song. I assume you weren't singing over the phone. I didn't quite understand what you meant here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were these people going to go? The MUP, from the police station at Kula, where this was all situated. Secondly, in the songs from the first Serb uprising in the periods of 1804 and 1813, in one of the songs, there is a reference to Karadjordje sending Turks back to Turkey, and there is a poetic licence there and there was reference to the fact in that poem actually, not a song, that whoever decided to embrace the Orthodox religion could have stayed. So there was no actual need to use this phrase here. It was a kind of romantic propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you are talking to someone and you are giving instructions to this person. Take them to Bascarsija on foot. And then you say, "For those who convert to the Orthodox faith, those can stay, those can stay, and if they are women and children." That's not what it was about. This was not an instruction you were giving anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, it was at night, in the evening. And everything that's being said in this propaganda, this is romantic language, and basically we have the population that left Butmir, and they can confirm what the relationship was and what treatment they received on that day. And I'm claiming that on that day, they left and they went where they wanted to go without any hassle, especially when we talk about the women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we have to stop for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour I have something I must raise for a minute, two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In the absence of the witness, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes in the absence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another Chamber needs this courtroom so it really has to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It will be quick, Your Honour, but in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Prstojevic out of the courtroom, but Mr. Prstojevic I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony you've given and which is about to be given. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in a sense a really stupid and trivial issue, but raising an important point. And I want to make it clear it's not some sort of childish squabble between Mr. Krajisnik and myself but it's this: I've handed to Mr. Krajisnik in the course of the morning that book of maps that we use for the case. Mr. Krajisnik doesn't want to give it back because he says that it's his case and so on. The fact is, Your Honour, if I -- I am not slighted, I'm not humiliated by having the conduct of the case taken out of my hands to the degree it has been, but I am exasperated, fed up, and really truly frustrated by it, Your Honour. And this is an illustration of the small things. Mr. Krajisnik wishes to prepare his cross-examination. I've got to prepare my cross-examination. I'm just going to make a friendly request to the Prosecution straight away if we can have additional copies of that book but, Your Honour, this is going to happen time and time and time again. If we've got two people conducting the case then two people are going to have to be equipped to conduct the case. Your Honour, it's getting absolutely ridiculous but, Your Honour, if I can not conduct the case as counsel and if I can not retain my own practical equipment to conduct the case as counsel and continue in this way, Your Honour, I will not continue to conduct the case until I am supplied with the tools to do it and allowed to do my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did you receiver from Mr. Stewart a copy of the book of maps?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, each and every one of us got this book. This is my book. I brought it along this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did you receive a copy of the book of maps from Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I gave mine to him this morning to photocopy it. I brought it from the prison. This is a mistake. Each and every one of us got a copy of these maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, is there any possibility that Mr. Krajisnik in the past received a copy of this book of which you he would like to keep his own personal copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll sort this out. I physically handed it to Mr. Krajisnik. I have asked and instructed that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's let one thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is brought to court all the time. If it's not here I apologise for sorting it out. My exasperation remains, Your Honour, at the situation. But if we have made a mistake and there is confusion in relation to this map, then I heartily apologise. I've got a zillion things to do including all thee negotiations and these financial matters and so on, Your Honour. The last thing I want to do is to be troubled with whether I can lay my hands on my book of maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think one thing will be perfectly clear. If you provide a copy of the book of maps to Mr. Krajisnik, who does not have one, and if Mr. Krajisnik would like to have one or some of these maps available to him in preparing for the next court hearing, then, under those circumstances, the solution would not be not to return it to you but to see that a copy is made and if the Chamber can be of assistance, under those circumstances, I'm not saying that these are the circumstances but if that would be the circumstances, I would be happy to personally make the photocopy involved. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you for that help, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.
